name: The Humane League: cage-free corporate campaigns (charityevals)
summary: The Humane League (THL) runs corporate campaigns, in the US and through the 82-group Open Wing Alliance worldwide, that get food companies to stop buying eggs from caged hens and then hold them to those promises. This model covers that cage-free work, about 60% of THL's 2025 program spending: we estimate about 6.3 suffering-adjusted days averted per dollar, roughly 1.6× GiveDirectly at the site's default exchange rates. Most of the very wide range comes from the shared exchange rate between animal suffering and human wellbeing; among THL-specific inputs, the biggest uncertainties are THL's share of credit among the groups campaigning on the same companies (20–65%), how many years earlier accountability pressure gets hens out of cages (1–6), and THL's own, undefined count of hens spared. Broiler-chicken campaigns and policy work are not modelled.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What THL's cage-free corporate campaigns (US and global, including Open Wing Alliance grants) cost in 2025, with their share of management and fundraising. From the 2025 audited financial statements and the annual report's split by program area.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many hens a year are in the supply chains THL's 2025 work moved: new cage-free commitments it secured, and hens that left cages in 2025 at companies it held to earlier promises. Both are THL's own counts.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: How much suffering one hen is spared each year she lives cage-free instead of caged, and how many years earlier the switch happens because of the campaign.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, switches that would have happened on schedule anyway, credit shared with the many other groups campaigning on the same companies, and companies not following through. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: Suffering-adjusted days (SADs) averted, per dollar of the cage-free program's full cost.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With salary sacrifice counted, your dollar is credited with its share only.

rows.label: Program expenses (all programs), 2025

source.title: THL audited financial statements 2025, Statement of Functional Expenses
source.page: p. 5, Statement of Functional Expenses, Program Services column

rows.explainer: Program-service expenses for the year ended 31 December 2025, from the audited statements. It includes the $4.26M of grants THL made: to Open Wing Alliance (OWA) member groups abroad, to Animal Policy Alliance members in the US, and $2.15M to The Humane League UK (note 7). The Form 990 gives $14,619,381 for the same line.

rows.label: Total expenses (all programs, management, fundraising), 2025

source.title: THL audited financial statements 2025, Statement of Functional Expenses
source.page: p. 5, Statement of Functional Expenses, 2025 Total column

rows.explainer: Total operating expenses for 2025: programs $14.62M, management and general $4.30M, fundraising $2.69M. The Form 990 total ($21,682,964) is $73k higher because it also counts investment fees.

rows.label: Share of program spending that goes to cage-free corporate campaigns
rows.explainer:
THL doesn't split its spending by campaign, so this share is ours. The 2025 annual report (p. 17, preliminary) splits program spending into Global Programs $5.20M (36%, including the THL UK grant), Education & Mobilization $4.66M (33%), US Public Policy & Corporate Engagement $2.50M (17%) and OWA & APA grants $1.99M (14%, of which $0.3M to the Animal Policy Alliance).

Best guess 60%: in 2025 nearly every campaign the report describes is about cages (Subway, Ahold Delhaize, Best Western, Walmart, the global egg-farm investigation, OWA's 234 new commitments), and most mobilization supported those campaigns. What is left out: policy and legislative work (APA grants, Prop 12 and EATS Act defence, the $2.5M US policy area is partly this), broiler-chicken campaigns, and plant-based outreach. The 2025 annual report and Form 990 don't mention broiler work, but THL's impact page says '140+ leading US businesses have committed to THL's science-based welfare standards for chickens raised for meat' (thehumaneleague.org/our-impact), so that program exists and carries ongoing accountability costs; how large it was in 2025 is unknown.

Low 45%: broiler, policy and THL UK work (UK campaigns start from enriched cages and include broilers) take more of the budget than the report's emphasis suggests; this end is speculative, as no source splits it. High 80%: almost all corporate and mobilization work in 2025 was cage-free.

rows.label: Spending on cage-free corporate campaigns, 2025
rows.explainer: Program expenses times the cage-free share above. It includes the cage-free part of OWA grants and of the THL UK grant, because the hens counted under Reach include those groups' wins.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programs in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do. At 1.48 THL's overhead is on the high side for an advocacy group: management and general was $4.30M in 2025.

rows.label: Cost of the cage-free program, including overhead
rows.explainer: The full 2025 cost of the work that produced the hen counts below. One year's spending is set against one year's results; in steady state, this year's spending produces next year's wins much as last year's produced this year's.

rows.label: Hens covered by new cage-free commitments THL secured in 2025

source.title: THL 2025 Annual Report
source.quote: 1.6M HENS IMPACTED by 4 companies' new commitments to end cages in their supply chains

rows.explainer: Hens (standing flock) in the supply chains of the four companies that made new cage-free commitments to THL in 2025. The Form 990 (Part III) gives the same figure. THL's own count: it doesn't publish the companies' egg volumes or the conversion to hens, so we can't check it. The 234 new commitments won by OWA member groups worldwide aren't counted here (no hen figure is published), which makes this row conservative. Range ±25% (1.2M–2.0M) for THL's unpublished conversion from egg volumes to hens.

rows.label: Hens moved out of cages in 2025 by accountability work (THL and OWA)

source.title: THL 2025 Annual Report
source.quote: 7.5M HENS SPARED from cages around the globe

rows.explainer:
THL reports '7.5M HENS SPARED from cages around the globe' for 2025 (annual report p. 3) and, per its 2024 Form 990 (Part III), 'WE SPARED 4.6 MILLION HENS FROM CAGES GLOBALLY' in 2024, 'AND SECURED COMMITMENTS TO FREE AN ADDITIONAL 79 MILLION MORE' (2024 Form 990, assets.ctfassets.net/ww1ie0z745y7/1AXdVUjWnPoagK2mQbnvyQ/…AMENDED_990…pdf). The 2025 report's '162.5M MORE EVERY YEAR' against 2024's '79 MILLION MORE' looks like a running total, which makes reading (b) below plausible. THL doesn't publish what these count. Two readings: (a) hens newly out of cages during the year at companies THL and OWA members pressured, giving 7.5M for 2025; (b) a running total of hens spared at those companies, so 2025 added only 7.5M − 4.6M = 2.9M. THL's 4.6M for 2024 is also larger than the OWA's own count of hens at companies reporting progress that year (3.3M, 85 companies), so THL's figure is a broader measure than company-reported progress.

Because the definition is unpublished, this is our judgment: best 6.0M, nearer the annual reading, because a running total of only 4.6M by 2024 would be small next to the ~100M hens the US cage-free flock gained from 2016 to 2024 and to single 2024 wins THL reports (CKE, about 1.3M hens); low 2.9M (cumulative reading); high 7.5M (annual reading). Examples in the report: The Cheesecake Factory reporting 100% cage-free (nearly 185,000 hens); Subway committing to finish its US switch ahead of its deadline (nearly 340,000 hens; this may also be among the four new commitments, see share_not_yet_compliant). Top-down check: USDA's US cage-free flock grew from 125.9M hens (Dec 2024, https://esmis.nal.usda.gov/sites/default/release-files/rj4304553/mw22x155b/3x818g120/PYMCAGEFREE.PDF) to 151.6M (Oct 2026), about 14M a year, so even 7.5M worldwide is not more than exist; it doesn't confirm THL's count.

rows.label: Hens per year in the supply chains THL's 2025 work moved
rows.explainer: New commitments plus hens moved out of cages under accountability pressure. Hens are counted as standing flock, so one hen here is one hen-year of cage-free housing for each year the change lasts. The two kinds of hens have different counterfactuals, so years, follow-through and counterfactual are set per branch below and combined, weighted by hen-years, into the canonical rows.

rows.label: Share of those hens still caged when the work happened
rows.explainer: Hens already out of cages before the campaign can't be credited to it. Both counts are meant to be of caged hens, so the best guess is close to 1. We take 90% for overlap and double counting: the same hens can appear in both counts (Subway's early-switch commitment, nearly 340,000 hens, is plausibly both one of the four new commitments and an accountability win: about 4% of reach), and a hen counted as spared may reappear in a later report. Supply already cage-free when a company commits is in counterfactual_new_commitments, and uncertainty about how THL defines its hen counts is in the range on accountability_hens, not here. Low 70%: substantial overlap. High 100%: no overlap.

rows.label: Hens per year the campaign can change
rows.explainer: Hens per year whose housing the 2025 work could change.

rows.label: Share of counted hens starting in enriched (furnished) cages
rows.explainer: In the EU (since 2012) and the UK, caged hens are in enriched cages, where moving to cage-free spares less suffering than leaving a battery cage. THL's counts are worldwide and include OWA wins in Europe (summits in Portugal and Poland, Best Western pressured 'from Peru to Poland', a Bulgarian cage farm shut) and THL UK's work ($2.15M grant). The named 2025 wins are mostly US (Subway, Cheesecake Factory, Ahold Delhaize), and more than a quarter of OWA's 234 new commitments in 2025 were in Africa (60+), where cages are battery cages. Best 15%. Low 5%: almost all US and Global South. High 30%: Europe is a large share of the 'around the globe' count.

rows.label: Suffering averted by leaving an enriched cage, relative to leaving a battery cage

source.title: Welfare Footprint Project, laying hens (Schuck-Paim & Alonso 2021)
source.quote: 1,410 hours of Hurtful pain and 4,065 hours of Annoying pain prevented for each hen

rows.explainer: Welfare Footprint estimates that a hen kept in an aviary instead of a conventional (battery) cage avoids at least 275 hours of disabling, 2,313 of hurtful and 4,645 of annoying pain over her laying life; instead of a furnished (enriched) cage, 1,410 hours of hurtful and 4,065 of annoying pain, with no disabling-pain gain reported. SADs weight disabling pain far more than hurtful or annoying pain, so the enriched-cage gain is a small fraction of the battery-cage gain. Best 25%. Low 10%: the gain is almost all in the lightest pain categories. High 60%: the hurtful-pain ratio (1,410 / 2,313 ≈ 0.61), if disabling pain matters less than SAD weights say. We use this ratio rather than the repo's enriched-to-aviary fact because that fact is sourced from an evaluator model that was blinded in this build.

rows.label: SADs averted per hen-year moved out of cages (battery/enriched blend)
rows.explainer: The shared figure for a hen moving from a battery cage to an aviary (17.5 suffering-adjusted days averted per hen-year, low 7.9, from Ambitious Impact's SADs), blended with the smaller gain for hens starting in enriched cages (EU, UK): battery share × full gain + enriched share × gain ratio. Cage-free barns rather than aviaries, and the higher keel-fracture and pecking rates in some cage-free flocks, are covered by the fact's range and by the evidence adjustment.

rows.label: Years a new commitment brings cage-free housing forward
rows.explainer: How many years earlier hens under a commitment won in 2025 leave cages than without the campaign. Anchor: Rethink Priorities' movement-wide estimate for corporate chicken commitments, 4 to 36 years (mean 15), measured against a world with no campaigns since 2005 and ending when legislation or market change would have caused the reform anyway. We take 10, below RP's mean, because commitments won in 2025 arrive when 46% of the US flock is already cage-free, several US states require it by law, and cage-free is spreading in Europe and Latin America, so the market would get there sooner than in RP's comparison. Many 2025 commitments are in Africa and Asia, where cages are still the norm, which is why we don't go lower. RP's 4–36 range is kept as the low and high ends.

rows.label: Years earlier hens leave cages because of accountability pressure
rows.explainer: For hens at companies that had already promised to go cage-free, the gain is how much earlier they leave cages than if no group had followed up, averaged over all counted hens: zero for companies that would have switched on schedule anyway (deadline-driven, or in US states whose laws require cage-free: California, Massachusetts, Colorado, Michigan, Washington, Oregon, Nevada, Arizona, Utah), several years for laggards that would have kept slipping (Walmart had been silent for four years). This row carries the whole counterfactual for this branch, so it isn't discounted again in counterfactual_adj. Best 3 years: 92% of commitments due by 2024 were fulfilled (OWA; the basis, companies or volume, isn't stated), so most companies switch within a few years of their deadline; follow-up moves the slow ones forward by a few years and keeps some from dropping out. Low 1: mostly hurries companies that were about to switch. High 6: without follow-up many pledges would have lapsed for years, in line with RP's lower end (4 years) for commitments themselves. Reference points: The Cheesecake Factory, under THL pressure, reported going 100% cage-free 'six years ahead of schedule' (annual report p. 10), an upper-end case for a single company; the Animal Welfare Observatory model in this repo (imported from ACE) assumes accountability campaigning brings companies forward by 2–2.5 years in two programs (implementation in 1.5–3 years instead of 4–5) and by 15 years in a third (10 instead of 25).

rows.label: Discounted years, new commitments
rows.explainer: Years brought forward by new commitments, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted years, accountability
rows.explainer: Years brought forward by accountability work, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Years the move out of cages is brought forward
rows.explainer: Hen-weighted average of the two branches' years (10 for new commitments, 3 for accountability), shown for comparison with other models. The calculation uses the discounted years of each branch (next row).

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
rows.explainer: Hen-weighted average of the two branches' discounted years. Combined with the hen-year-weighted follow-through and counterfactual below, it reproduces the sum of the two branches exactly.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: How far to trust that moving hens out of cages averts the suffering the SAD figure says. Uncertainty about THL's hen counts is in the range on accountability_hens and overlap in share_not_yet_compliant, so this row is about welfare in practice only: barn and aviary flocks have more keel-bone fractures and injurious pecking than cage flocks (Welfare Footprint notes cage-free systems are not yet as technologically mature as cages), and some 'cage-free' systems are crowded barns rather than aviaries. Best 0.85. Low 0.6: the cage-free systems hens actually move into are markedly worse than the aviaries SADs assume. High 1.0: SADs already capture it. A cage-free campaign rests on observable company sourcing, so it deserves more trust than diet-change outreach, which relies on self-reported behaviour.

rows.label: Share of new-commitment hens that wouldn't have gone cage-free without campaigns

source.title: Rethink Priorities (Šimčikas 2019)
source.quote: 18–26% of eggs would have been cage-free without campaigns (US); 20–50% outside the US

rows.explainer: Share of hens under new 2025 commitments that would not have gone cage-free without campaigns. Anchor: RP estimates 18–26% of US eggs and 20–50% outside the US would have been cage-free without any campaigns (1 − share: 0.5–0.82). We take 0.65, below RP's middle, because RP's comparison is a world with no campaigns since 2005, while in 2025 the market and laws already push a larger share of supply cage-free on their own. Supply that was already cage-free when the company committed is in this row; share_not_yet_compliant only covers counting overlaps between the two branches. Applies to the new-commitment branch only.

rows.label: Share of these switches that campaigning changed at all
rows.explainer: The share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway, weighted by each branch's discounted hen-years after follow-through. New commitments: 65% not cage-free anyway (anchored on RP). Accountability: 100% here, because hens that would have switched on schedule anyway already count for zero years in years_accountability; counting laws and deadlines here as well would discount them twice. At the best guesses this works out to 0.88.
rows.formula: (new_commitment_hens * discounted_years_new * follow_through_new * counterfactual_new_commitments + accountability_hens * discounted_years_accountability * follow_through_accountability) / (new_commitment_hens * discounted_years_new * follow_through_new + accountability_hens * discounted_years_accountability * follow_through_accountability)

rows.label: THL's share of credit, shared with other groups
rows.explainer:
Cage-free campaigns are run by coalitions. THL leads some US campaigns (Subway, Ahold Delhaize) but works alongside Mercy For Animals, Animal Equality, the Humane Society of the US and others, and the 7.5M hens 'around the globe' include wins by OWA member groups that THL funds and coordinates but doesn't run. THL itself counts its 'role in an inherently collaborative farmed animal protection movement' (annual report p. 16).

Best 40%: THL is the coordinator and largest funder of OWA and the lead group on its own US targets, but other groups share most global wins. Low 20%: THL is one of five or so comparable contributors. High 65%: most of the hens counted come from THL-led campaigns and OWA wins that wouldn't exist without THL's grants and training.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: With full credit for shared outcomes switched on, THL gets the whole outcome.

rows.label: Share of new commitments honoured
rows.explainer: RP's range for the share of cage-free commitments that will be honoured (US 33–85%, outside the US 63–90%). RP assumes no further compliance spending; THL does spend on compliance, but that work and its cost are counted in the accountability branch, so we keep RP's range here. Best 65%, near its middle.

rows.label: Share of reported switches that stick
rows.explainer: For hens a company has already reported moving out of cages, the remaining risk is reversal (companies backsliding during egg shortages, as some did during the 2022–2025 avian-flu price spikes) or partial reporting. Whether THL's count is right in the first place is in the range on accountability_hens. Best 95%; low 85% (noticeable backsliding); high 100%.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (companies following through)
rows.explainer: Follow-through, weighted by each branch's discounted hen-years: 65% of new commitments honoured (RP) and 95% of reported switches sticking. At the best guesses about 0.82, because new commitments carry more hen-years per hen (10 years vs 3).
rows.formula: (new_commitment_hens * discounted_years_new * follow_through_new + accountability_hens * discounted_years_accountability * follow_through_accountability) / (new_commitment_hens * discounted_years_new + accountability_hens * discounted_years_accountability)

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above: about 0.24 at the best guesses. Not adjusted for: indirect effects of THL's work on norms and future campaigns, OWA's 234 new commitments with unpublished hen counts, broiler and policy work (left out of both cost and outcome), and harm from poorly run cage-free barns beyond what evidence_adj covers.

rows.label: SADs averted
rows.explainer: Hens per year changed × discounted years the change is brought forward × suffering averted per hen-year × adjustments.

rows.label: SADs averted per dollar
rows.explainer: Suffering-adjusted days averted per dollar of the cage-free program's full cost.

rows.label: Salaries and benefits, 2025

source.title: THL audited financial statements 2025, Statement of Functional Expenses
source.page: p. 5, Statement of Functional Expenses, Salaries and benefits row

rows.explainer: All salaries, benefits and payroll taxes in 2025 across programs, management and fundraising (Form 990 Part IX lines 5–10: $11,667,680; 232 employees during the year).

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of total cost
rows.explainer: Salaries and benefits ÷ total expenses, both from the audited statements: 54%.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable for-profit jobs
rows.explainer: How much less THL staff earn than in comparable for-profit roles (campaigners, organisers, communications, operations). The repo's reference class is about 35% for advocacy groups (15% for large delivery charities), and the other corporate-campaign models use 35% with a high end of 55%; we use the same. Low 15%: THL's US salaries for senior roles are close to market. High 55%: most staff are organisers and campaigners who could earn far more in corporate communications or sales.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff (in-kind donation)
rows.explainer: What staff give up, applied to the cage-free program's cost.

rows.label: Share of the full cost paid by cash donations
rows.explainer: With salary sacrifice counted, cash donations pay for this share of the full cost.

rows.label: SADs averted per dollar you give
rows.explainer: The bottom line: suffering-adjusted days averted per dollar donated, after crediting staff with their share.

output.label: SADs averted per dollar you give
